parts:
Aidan--

This is not straightforward to intuit, because of the presence of f5, f6 and f7 as additional predictors along with higher_f. They may create their own collinearity issues shaping the values of regression coefficients. Without them, though, your dv1 is just another dependent loading on higher_f, and higher_f becomes what is common to f1-f4 AND dv1. The presence of additional predictors of dv1 (all, presumably, free to correlate with higher_f), complicates the interpretation.

If you regressed dv1 on f1-f4, those coefficients may be misleading because of the collinearity. If you excluded f5-f7 from that model, the coefficients may be biased due to excluded predictors. You would be better off guessing from zero order correlations between the factors.

To function well as a higher order factor, there needs to be not just high covariance among f1-f4 but a pattern to their correlations with other variables. Estimate a CFA including f1-f7 and dv1. See if proportionality constraints hold across f1-f4. In particular, if x1 and x2 are two indicators of the same factor, and x3 is any other variable in the model it must be true that:

correlation (x1, x3) / correlation (x2, x3) = k

a constant across ALL other variables in the model. If this is not so, then the factor model is not correct (without such devices as cross-loadings or residual covariance). Lack of fit due to the higher order factor structure may also create misleading regression coefficients.



On Mon, Oct 26, 2020 at 12:28 PM Aiden <aide...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi all, 

I would like some help with understanding the variance of higher order factors when being used as a predictor in SEM. Without putting in my whole model, an example is below. 

I have 8 predictors, of which 4 loads onto a higher order factor and one dv.

An example: 

'f1  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
f2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6
f3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9
f4 =~ x10 + x11 + x12
f5 =~ x13 + x14 + x15
f6 =~ x16 + x17 + x18
f7 =~ x19 + x20 + x21
f8 =~ x22 + x23 + x4

higher_f =~ f1 + f2 + f3 + f4

dv1 ~ higher_f + f5 + f6 + f7'


I know that both f1 and f2 have positive significant coefficients with dv1 (tested it without higher-order factors), while f3 and f4 are nonsignificant coefficients with dv1. 
I used a higher-order factor because f1-f4 are all very highly positively correlated with each other. However, the higher_f factor turned into a negative relationship with dv1 instead of a positive relationship. I am not sure why this would be the case as I would have expected a positive relationship between higher_f and dv. I would appreciate some guidance.

Kind regards,
Aiden
